item.title: Attorney General Bonta Secures District Court Victory Denying Trump Administration’s TRO, Building on Earlier Appellate Win to Protect California Elections
item.description:
October 28, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today issued the following statement after the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California denied the Trump Administration’s request for a temporary restraining order (TRO) that would have required California election officials to segregate and not count mail-in ballots returned by approximately 20,000 individuals the administration “believes” are “likely” noncitizens, but has also admitted could include several U.S. citizens. Attorney General Bonta filed a brief opposing the TRO, a supplemental brief further opposing the TRO, and a motion to dismiss the federal government’s lawsuit. Today’s district court victory builds on Monday’s win at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, which rejected the administration’s attempt to obtain emergency relief by bypassing the district court.

“No administration can disenfranchise thousands of individuals or disrupt an ongoing election based on highly unreliable claims of noncitizenship,” said Attorney General Rob Bonta. “Today’s ruling is yet another important victory for the rule of law and the right to vote. But this fight is not over. We will keep fighting to protect California’s elections from unlawful federal interference and get this baseless lawsuit dismissed.”

“For the second day this week, our country’s legal system is standing up to the President’s authoritarian attempts to remain in power unchecked and unchallenged. For more than a year, California’s sovereignty has been under siege, and this lawsuit is his latest attack on the rule of law, the California Constitution, and the U.S. Constitution,” said Governor Gavin Newsom. “California will continue to deliver a free and fair election that follows both state and federal law, as the Judicial Branch — importantly a co-equal branch of government — is deciding in real time, much to the Trump Administration’s dismay.”

In opposing the administration’s request for a TRO, Attorney General Bonta argued that the court should deny the request because it would:

  • Lack a legal basis: The administration has no legal basis to force California to segregate and not count ballots based on unverified claims about citizenship.
  • Risk disenfranchising eligible voters: The administration’s list could include eligible voters, and the administration has not provided California with the underlying data and methodology needed to evaluate its validity.
  • Violate federal and state law: The administration’s demands would conflict with federal laws protecting voting rights and California laws governing elections.
  • Disrupt an ongoing election: Requiring California to change its ballot-counting procedures in the middle of an election would disrupt the election and create unnecessary confusion for election officials and voters.

The district court agreed with all those arguments, decisively rejecting the federal government’s motion.

In the order, the court observed that “[e]roded trust in our democracy is irreparable. Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process.” And it explained that “[p]oll taxes, literacy tests, and other obstacles [have been] used to prevent individuals from casting their vote. Every generation in our history has witnessed repeated clashes between those who seek to limit access to the ballot and those who fight to ensure it. In this case, the federal government seeks to segregate and exclude over 20,000 ballots. This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections. If Plaintiff’s last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process. Over 20,000 registered Californians would potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve. The Government’s Application for Temporary Restraining Order is DENIED.”

The Trump Administration’s latest attempt to interfere in California’s elections follows years of efforts to undermine election results and voting rights:

  • After losing the 2020 presidential election to Joe Biden, President Trump pressured Georgia officials to “find” 11,780 votes, fueled the January 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol as Congress certified Biden’s victory, and continues to falsely claim that he won the 2020 presidential election — even seizing ballots from that election in Fulton County, Georgia, in January 2026 as part of efforts to relitigate the results.
  • The Trump Administration sought to impose new restrictions on voting and election administration through executive orders that courts have found unlawful, including the recent U.S. Supreme Court ruling led by Attorney General Bonta blocking the administration’s attempts to seize control of mail voting nationwide.
  • In July 2026, the Trump Administration initially alleged that California had more than 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls, which the Trump Administration reduced to about 20,000 — a 90% decrease from their earlier allegations — before bringing this litigation. This mirrors the Trump Administration’s accusations against Nevada, where the Trump Administration initially claimed that Nevada had nearly 16,000 noncitizen voters. It later reduced that number to 185 voters and has not provided evidence to support its claim that all of the 185 individuals are noncitizens.

item.title: Attorney General Bonta: States Must Have the Ability to Protect Residents from Assault Rifles Commonly Used in Mass Shootings
item.description:
October 28, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

OAKLAND —  California Attorney General Rob Bonta today, as part of a coalition of 19 attorneys general, filed an amicus brief in the U.S. Supreme Court in support of laws enacted in Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois, restricting the sale, manufacture, and possession of certain uniquely dangerous assault rifles. The brief, filed in Viramontes v. County of Cook, urges the U.S. Supreme Court to uphold appellate court rulings that affirmed that these challenged assault weapon laws are consistent with the Second Amendment and the nation’s strong historical tradition of regulating weapons that are uniquely dangerous.

“The California Department of Justice will continue to aggressively defend life-saving safety measures and support local leaders with the tools necessary to keep people safe. Assault weapon laws restrict a small and uniquely dangerous category of weapons that have proven to be mass shooters’ weapon of choice for a reason,” said Attorney General Bonta. “California enacted the nation’s first state-level assault weapons restriction almost four decades ago to protect our residents from uniquely dangerous weapons with battlefield features that facilitate indiscriminate mass killing. The Supreme Court has the opportunity to affirm what many appellate courts have already found: these commonsense protections are reasonable and constitutional. A mass shooter with an assault weapon demonstrably can inflict more deaths and injuries compared to those using other weapons, and three-quarters of mass shootings of 10 or more victims from 2012 to 2022 involved the use of an assault weapon. Protecting our communities from mass shootings and gun violence is a core responsibility of state and local government.”

The coalition’s amicus brief explains that the AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles are uniquely dangerous because their features facilitate assaultive mass killing and are poorly designed for self-defense purposes. The brief also explains that the U.S. has a long historical tradition of regulating uniquely dangerous weapons. It also urges the Supreme Court to reject petitioners’ argument that the Second Amendment prohibits laws restricting any weapon, regardless of dangerousness, once it has reached some arbitrary popularity threshold. The brief argues this would be a dangerous, illogical, and ahistorical outcome that is contrary to the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment caselaw , and would also encourage firearms manufacturers to flood communities with new dangerous weapons before a legislature manages to institute restrictions to prevent them from proliferating in shootings and other criminal activity.

California has been a leader among states that have enacted effective firearm safety laws. Republican Governor George Deukmejian signed California’s initial bipartisan assault weapons restriction into law in 1989 following a hate-motivated school shooting at Cleveland Elementary School in Stockton, California, in which a gunman wielding an AK 47-style semiautomatic assault rifle with detachable 30-round and 75-round large-capacity magazines fired over 100 times in about three minutes — murdering five young children and injuring 30 other students and a teacher. A 2026 report from the California Department of Justice's Office of Gun Violence Prevention showed that California’s mass shooting victimization rate for 2023-2025 fell to 38% below the rate for the rest of the U.S. on average. Today, 10 other states and several cities generally restrict the sale, manufacture, and possession of assault rifles, including the AK-47 and AR-15. 

Connecticut enacted its initial assault weapons law in 1993 and expanded that law in 2013 following the December 2012 Sandy Hook elementary school shooting in which a gunman armed with an AR-15 style rifle and large capacity magazines fired over 150 rounds and murdered 20 children and six educators in under five minutes. 

Attorney General Bonta joins the attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Washington s in filing the brief.

A copy of the brief can be found here.

item.title: Attorney General Bonta Issues Statement on the Passing of Dolores Huerta
item.description:
October 28, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today issued a statement on the passing of labor and civil rights leader Dolores Huerta:  

“Dolores Huerta was a friend, a mentor, a source of inspiration and guidance, and a lifelong hero of mine. 

Her activism and inspiration touched countless lives, and her ongoing legacy will surely touch countless more in the years ahead. I’m grateful she had such an influence on my own life. From my early days growing up in the headquarters of the United Farmworkers of America, to my time in public office, she was a constant, firm, irresistible force for justice and needed change.

Her rallying cry “Sí Se Puede” perfectly encapsulated who she was — a woman full of fight and right who knew that if we worked together, there was nothing we couldn’t achieve.

There are not enough superlatives to describe her life, legacy, and the impact she had on our nation’s ongoing pursuit of justice and fairness. 

She helped shape the history of the farmworkers' movement and changed the face of the labor movement forever. She defined what it meant to own our power, use our voice, and ensure the people always remain the most potent force in our American democracy.

My deepest condolences to her family. This is a devastating loss for so many in the labor movement and across the nation.”

item.title: Attorney General Bonta Announces New Resources to Protect California Elections, Continues Urging Early Voting
item.description:
October 28, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

OAKLAND — With less than a week until the Tuesday, November 3, 2026, General Election, California Attorney General Rob Bonta today announced four new resources to help ensure California’s elections remain safe, fair, and secure: (1) a legal alert on California election law protections against seizures of election materials; (2) a law enforcement bulletin pursuant to Senate Bill (SB) 73, which was signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom earlier this year, that provides elections officials and election site managers with guidance on responding to law enforcement attempts to access election sites where ballots are cast, processed, or counted; (3) a law enforcement bulletin on protections for voters and poll workers against intimidation; and (4) a consumer alert warning about the prevalence of election-related misinformation and disinformation, especially involving artificial intelligence and social media.

Attorney General Bonta also urged Californians who have not yet voted to make a plan and cast their ballots as soon as possible. Every eligible California voter has received a ballot by mail and can return their completed ballot at an official drop box, mail it back, or vote in person before or on Election Day. To avoid potential postal delays, voters now are encouraged to use a drop box or vote in person. Voters who choose to mail their ballot should bring it to a post office counter and ask that it be postmarked. While the deadline to register to vote online has passed, eligible Californians can still register and vote in person through Same Day Voter Registration (Conditional Voter Registration).

“The Trump Administration is waging unprecedented attacks on our elections. California will not back down. We’re using every tool at our disposal, including new resources released today, to protect voters and defend our democracy from unlawful interference,” said Attorney General Bonta. “With Election Day just around the corner, I urge every Californian who hasn’t voted to make a plan and cast their ballot early. We will remain vigilant in defending the right to vote — the right from which all other rights flow.” 

The Attorney General enforces California’s election laws to ensure free and fair elections. In the lead-up to and on Election Day, the California Department of Justice will be on call to assist the Secretary of State’s Office in enforcing California’s election laws through a team of attorneys and administrative staff located across the state. For up-to-date information on how to vote, check official websites, including sos.ca.gov/elections. Voters can register to track their ballot and confirm that it is counted at wheresmyballot.sos.ca.gov.

Denial of voting rights can be reported in English through the Secretary of State’s confidential toll-free Voter Hotline at (800) 345-VOTE (8683). Other language options, including Spanish, Tagalog, and Chinese, are available. In addition, reports can be made via email at elections@sos.ca.gov.

Attorney General Bonta is firmly committed to protecting our elections and the right to vote. Earlier this week, he scored an early win when the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit rejected the Trump Administration’s attempt to force California to set aside more than 20,000 ballots from individuals it “believes” are “likely” noncitizens, based on highly unreliable claims of noncitizenship, without first obtaining a district court order. 

Publication #1: Legal Alert on Protections Against Seizure of Election Materials

The legal alert provides an overview of relevant California law regarding chain-of-custody and other strict requirements for handling ballots and elections materials, and provides recommended guidance to minimize disruption if any law enforcement official attempts to obtain a search warrant for ballots or other elections materials.

Publication #2: SB 73 Bulletin on Restrictions to Law Enforcement Access to Voting Sites

The bulletin explains how election officials should respond to law enforcement requests involving election sites and materials, including:

  • Provide Immediate Notice of Law Enforcement Investigations: Directs elections officials to immediately notify the Attorney General, Secretary of State, and county officials of law enforcement requests or attempts to access election sites.
  • Law Enforcement Presence at Election Sites: Explains federal and state restrictions on armed law enforcement and security personnel at polling places and limits on law enforcement interference with election administration.
  • Law Enforcement Access to Election Materials: Describes requirements for securely maintaining and preserving chain of custody of election records. It also explains restrictions on law enforcement access to or seizure of ballots, voter lists, certified voting technology, and other election materials.
  • Search Warrants: Explains the legal requirement for a judge-approved search warrant supported by probable cause and outlines procedures for notifying legal counsel, documenting searches, monitoring compliance with the warrant’s scope, and safeguarding election materials.

Publication #3: Law Enforcement Bulletin on Protections for Voters and Poll Workers Against Intimidation

This bulletin explains California laws that prohibit anyone, including law enforcement, from engaging in election interference, voter intimidation, and voter deception. For example:

  • It is a felony to use tactics of coercion or intimidation to induce or compel a person to vote or refrain from voting, or to vote or refrain from voting for any particular person or measure, at any election.
  • It is a felony to agree to vote in a certain way or induce others to vote in a certain way in exchange for money or something of value.

Publication #4: Consumer Alert on Misinformation’s Impact on Voting Rights

The consumer alert warns of prevalent sources of election misinformation — including artificial intelligence and social media — and explains how election misinformation can interfere with voting rights. California law makes it a crime to intentionally mislead voters about their eligibility to vote, or about where and when to vote.

item.title: California Department of Justice Releases Report on Officer-Involved Shooting of Brandon Salgado
item.description:
October 27, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta, pursuant to Assembly Bill 1506 (AB 1506), today released a report on the death of Brandon Salgado from an officer-involved shooting in Long Beach, California on April 26, 2024. The incident involved officers from the Long Beach Police Department (LBPD). The report is part of continuous efforts by the California Department of Justice (DOJ) to provide transparency and accountability in law enforcement practices. The report presents a comprehensive analysis of the incident that outlines DOJ’s findings. After a thorough investigation, DOJ concluded the evidence does not support filing criminal charges in this case.
 
“The loss of life is always tragic, and we hope that this report provides those personally affected and the Long Beach community clarity,” said Attorney General Bonta. “The California Department of Justice is committed to working with law enforcement agencies to foster a legal system that promotes fairness, transparency, and accountability for all. We believe it is our responsibility to create a safer California built on the foundation of trust and AB 1506 is fundamental in helping us achieve those goals.”
 
On April 26, 2024, an LBPD officer responded to a call of an “armed home invasion robbery.” Upon backup officers’ arrival, Mr. Salgado engaged in an hour-long standoff with LBPD, where he repeatedly stated he was armed, and pointed what appeared to be a gun at himself and eventually at the officers. After aiming the gun at LBPD, an officer then fired his weapon, fatally wounding Mr. Salgado. After the shooting, it was discovered that Mr. Salgado’s gun was a replica airsoft pistol.

AB 1506 requires DOJ to investigate all incidents of officer-involved shootings resulting in the death of an unarmed civilian in the state. After conducting a thorough investigation into this incident, DOJ concluded that the evidence does not show, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the officer involved acted without the intent to defend themselves and others from what they reasonably believed to be imminent death or serious bodily injury. Therefore, there is insufficient evidence to support a criminal prosecution of the officer, and no further action will be taken in this case.

As part of all AB 1506 investigations, DOJ meticulously examines each case to propose policy recommendations that it believes will help prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future. After a detailed investigation, DOJ has identified no policy recommendations in this case. 

Here is a copy of the report.

item.title: Attorney General Bonta Announces Reimbursement Process for Youth Unlawfully Issued Citations by the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department Through Student Citation Program
item.description:
October 27, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

Individuals who may be eligible can submit a claim through April 18, 2027

SAN BERNADINO — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today announced that under the California Department of Justice’s (DOJ) recent settlement with the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department (Sheriff's Department), individuals who were cited by the Sheriff's Department when they were under the age of 18 for certain offenses under a student citation program may be eligible for reimbursement of any related fines and fees and dismissal of the citation. The settlement formally concludes practices associated with Operation CleanSWEEP (CleanSWEEP), a student citation program operating in San Bernardino County, and in several school districts across the County, from 1997 until 2022. Shortly after DOJ's investigation began in 2022, the Sheriff's Department suspended CleanSWEEP and it terminated the program countywide in January 2024.

“All students deserve school environments centered on their learning, not environments that criminalize youth. During a years-long investigation, my office found San Bernadino County’s CleanSWEEP program unlawfully issued citations to students that at times led to steep fines and resulted in adverse impacts against protected student groups,” said Attorney General Bonta. “Upon bringing these findings to the attention of law enforcement and school officials, the parties took significant steps to collaboratively address our findings, including by agreeing to permanently terminate the CleanSWEEP program. As part of my office’s settlement with the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department, students who were cited by the Sheriff's Department for certain offenses when they were under the age of 18 may be eligible for dismissal of the citation and reimbursement of any related fines and fees. I encourage people who may be eligible to submit a claim to the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department by April 18, 2027."

ELIGIBILITY

If you were cited by the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department when you were under the age of 18 for certain offenses, you may be eligible for reimbursement of any related fines and fees and dismissal of the citation. You may be eligible for relief if you paid any fines and fees or have matters currently pending related to a citation for any of the following offenses: 

  • Daytime loitering on school grounds, under San Bernardino County Ordinance section 25.0202, Rancho Cucamonga Municipal Code section 9.30.030, Ontario Municipal Code section 5-7.04, or any similar ordinance (citation must have been issued on or after December 20, 2002).
  • A tobacco-related offense, under Penal Code section 308, subdivision (b) (citation must have been issued on or after June 9, 2016).
  • Fighting or disturbing the peace on school grounds, under Penal Code section 415.
  • Any offense if you were under the age of 12 (citation must have been issued on or after January 1, 2019).

If you received a citation listed above, you may be eligible for (1) reimbursement for any fines or fees relating to the citation, and (2) dismissal of the citation.

HOW TO SEEK REIMBURSEMENT FOR YOUR CITATION OR DISMISSAL OF YOUR CITATION

If you believe you received a citation listed above and may be eligible for relief, contact the Sheriff’s Department by:

  • Email: crcoordinator@sbcsd.org
  • Phone: 909-387-3406
  • Mail: 655 East 3rd St., San Bernardino, CA 92415 to the attention of Miles Kowalski. 

TTY callers may call the Department’s non-emergency dispatch lines: Valley Communications Center (VCC) at 909-387- 8313; and Desert Communications Center at 760-956-5001. 

All requests must be received by April 18, 2027.

Be prepared to provide proof of the citation, any related fines or fees, and any related pending matters. If you are not able to provide proof, the Sheriff’s Department will work with you to verify the information above. If you need reasonable accommodations related to your request, please contact the San Bernardino County Public Access ADA Coordinator by phone at 909-386-8655 or 7-1-1, or mail at 22 West Hospitality Lane, 3rd floor, San Bernardino, CA 92415.

THE CLEANSWEEP PROGRAM

CleanSWEEP — an acronym for “Success with Education/Enforcement Partnership” — was a youth-ticketing program developed by the Sheriff's Department in collaboration with schools and other law enforcement agencies across San Bernardino County. As part of the program, law enforcement agencies trained school staff to conduct investigations and issue citations to students for low-level offenses allegedly committed by students ages 10 through 17 on school campuses. Law enforcement agencies would later sign the citation and require students and their parents to appear in adult traffic court, typically without legal representation, where they faced potential serious penalties, including fines in some cases in excess of $1,000 for a single violation, and steeper penalties if students and their families failed to appear. From 2016 to 2022, the two most common cited violations countywide were for possession of under an ounce of marijuana (35%) and daytime loitering (34%).

ABOUT THE INVESTIGATION AND SETTLEMENTS

In 2022, DOJ began investigating the CleanSWEEP program and found, among other things, in implementing the program, the Sheriff's Department and Chaffey Joint Union High School District (the District) violated the law by issuing citations to students not authorized by law, such as for daytime loitering on school grounds, disturbing the peace on school grounds, and tobacco possession. DOJ’s investigation revealed the parties’ implementation of CleanSWEEP harmed protected student groups. Last month, Attorney General Bonta entered into two separate settlements reached cooperatively with the Sheriff's Department and the District. The settlements formally terminate practices associated with CleanSWEEP — which the Sheriff's Department and District independently suspended in 2022. 

Under the settlements, both parties agree to terms that include revised training and policy as well as monitoring to ensure compliance with the settlement. The Sheriff's Department and the District have already made progress in implementing their respective settlement terms. The Sheriff's Department has already made significant changes, including revising policies and procedures, revising training materials, agreeing to a training expert to help develop additional Student Resource Officer (SRO)-specific training, developing an SRO Guide, and agreeing to a data expert to analyze the Sheriff's Department citation and Racial and Identity Profiling Act (RIPA) data.

The District, in place of punitive citation practices, has invested in trauma-informed strategies, restorative justice training, mental health support, enhanced student services, and campus-wide supports that focus on education, engagement, and accountability. "Our collaboration with the Attorney General’s Office in discontinuing use of the county-wide program was rooted in shared values. This agreement reflects the District’s proactive efforts and our ongoing commitment to helping students grow in a safe, caring, and supportive school environment,” District Superintendent Dr. Mathew Holton stated.

item.title: Attorney General Bonta Sues Trump Administration for Rolling Back Financial Crime Enforcement
item.description:
October 27, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today joined a coalition of 21 attorneys general in filing a lawsuit challenging rulemaking by the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) regarding the Corporate Transparency Act. FinCEN’s recent rule permanently removes Beneficial Ownership Information (BOI) reporting requirements for U.S. companies and U.S. persons, a requirement intended to stop shell companies — often used to further illicit criminal activity, like money laundering or drug trafficking — from hiding their financial transactions from law enforcement. Today’s lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Oregon, alleges FinCEN’s new rule is in excess of statutory authority, contrary to law, and arbitrary and capricious, in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act and the U.S. Constitution. 

“The Trump Administration is unlawfully rolling back reporting requirements meant to help law enforcement track down bad actors who hide financial assets in shell companies. These anonymous accounts are often used for illegal activity — like by cartels and criminals to money launder, traffic drugs, or to hide bribes or illegal kickbacks,” said Attorney General Bonta. “Congress passed the Corporate Transparency Act with bipartisan support because it understood law enforcement needed an important additional tool to root out illegal financial transactions and corruption. My office is committed to supporting law enforcement’s efforts to enforce the laws that keep people safe and hold bad actors accountable.” 

The Corporate Transparency Act requires companies to report BOI to FinCEN to stop shell companies from hiding their financial transactions from law enforcement. The law was specifically intended to prevent the illicit use of shell companies by giving law enforcement agencies access to information about the ownership structures of shell companies. The Corporate Transparency Act requires beneficial owners to submit their names, addresses, birth dates and up-to-date identification records, like a passport or driver’s license, to FinCEN. This information is then later shared with law enforcement.

FinCEN’s new rule exempts all U.S. companies and individuals from reporting requirements and also exempts foreign companies from the requirement to report any U.S. persons who are beneficial owners. FinCEN claims that collecting information from these entities does not serve the public interest. In the new rule, FinCEN also commits to deleting all information previously reported by U.S. companies and individuals, records that likely include evidence of unsolved crimes.

In California, the California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation, the state’s financial services and consumer protection regulator, would have had access to FinCEN’s BOI for investigative and regulatory purposes if not for the promulgation of the new rule. FinCEN’s rule will force law enforcement and regulatory agencies that would have used FinCEN's BOI to instead resort to time-consuming, less reliable, and less successful procedures to obtain such information. In addition, states will be unable to use this information to enforce compliance with state tax laws, thereby depriving states of tax revenues that they would otherwise be able to collect.  

In filing this lawsuit, Attorney General Bonta joins the attorneys general of Oregon, Illinois, Arizona, Colorado, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Rhode Island, Virginia, Washington, and Wisconsin.

item.title: Attorney General Bonta Files Lawsuit Against Chiquita Canyon Landfill to Force Accountability for Environmental Contamination
item.description:
October 27, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

LOS ANGELES — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today, alongside the California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC), filed a lawsuit against Waste Connections, and other owners and operators of the Chiquita Canyon Landfill, related to the ongoing subsurface elevated temperature event that is the source of persistent environmental contamination, including repeated releases of contaminated liquids known as leachate, which can have profound impacts to public health. Chiquita Canyon is a 639-acre landfill located in the Santa Clarita Valley in Los Angeles County that opened in 1972. Since at least May 2022, the subsurface elevated temperate event has caused odors, large volumes of leachate, and other environmental impacts resulting from the rapid breakdown of the waste mass in the landfill. During this time, Chiquita Canyon has repeatedly and pervasively failed to manage hazardous waste at the landfill, in violation of state laws meant to protect people and the environment from hazards like the leachate being produced at the landfill. There has been consistent evidence of leaks, seeps, and spills of hazardous leachate and improper transport, treatment, and storage of hazardous materials. These failures are unlawful, have caused environmental harm, and threaten further environmental harm still. These violations, and the fact that they are continuing to happen, have led to today’s lawsuit. This suit, which follows several important administrative and court enforcement actions from other state and federal agencies, seeks to address the continuing impacts of the subsurface elevated temperature event.

“Protecting the environment and safeguarding Californians requires quick and effective action from the Chiquita Canyon Landfill’s owners and operators. For too long, the Chiquita Canyon Landfill has done the opposite, which has resulted in numerous spills of leachate and other violations of our state’s hazardous waste laws. We cannot allow the California dream to be smothered by the repeated releases of hazardous waste at the Chiquita Canyon Landfill — we must act,” said Attorney General Rob Bonta. “Other public agencies and residents have taken their own enforcement actions, and today my office is taking additional action to protect and defend the integrity of this region. Let there be no doubt, when owners and operators fail to do their part in protecting our water, soil, and air, my office will step in.” 

“Waste Connections has repeatedly, consistently and pervasively failed to lawfully manage hazardous waste at the Chiquita Canyon Landfill,” said California Environmental Protection Secretary Yana Garcia. “This lawsuit makes it clear that California will continue to hold Waste Connections accountable for its actions.”  

“For the people who live near this facility, and for all Californians, Waste Connections must manage hazardous waste safely and in full compliance with the law, clean up existing contamination and prevent future harm,” said DTSC Director Katherine Butler. “Today’s action is another important step toward addressing the magnitude of impacts and sends a clear message that this kind of waste mismanagement has serious consequences.”

“For years, families living near Chiquita Canyon Landfill have endured dangerous conditions, toxic gasses, and serious impacts to their health and safety, while those responsible have repeatedly failed to protect our community. No company should be allowed to put its profits ahead of the health of our families or the safety of our community,” said Assemblywoman Pilar Schiavo (D-Los Angeles). “I want to thank Attorney General Bonta and the DTSC for taking this critical step to hold the landfill accountable and enforce the laws meant to protect us. We deserve real relief from this ongoing public health crisis, and thanks to the action being taken today and the years of endless dedication from the impacted families, we are one big step closer.” 

What is Happening at the Chiquita Canyon Landfill?

The Chiquita Canyon Landfill is a 639-acre municipal solid waste disposal facility in Los Angeles County that is operated by Chiquita Canyon, LLC and its parent companies. The landfill stopped accepting waste on January 1, 2025, when it failed to obtain a permit from the Los Angeles Regional Water Quality Control Water Board (Regional Water Board). The subsurface elevated temperatures at the landfill started in May 2022, and the affected area has expanded from 20 acres to at least 90 acres. The subsurface elevated temperatures beneath the landfill, which have exceeded 212 degrees Fahrenheit in places, and have reached as high as 260 degrees Fahrenheit, result from chemical reactions that release odors, toxic fumes, and cause other environmental and health impacts. The reaction also produces millions of gallons of leachate that must be pumped out of the reaction area, collected, and disposed of properly as hazardous waste. The leachate has been found to contain benzene and, on occasion, methyl ethyl ketone, dangerous chemicals that can harm public health and the environment. On numerous occasions, the landfill has mismanaged the collection and removal of the leachate. For example, on November 14, 2025, the landfill spilled 8,000 gallons of hazardous leachate, which flowed into the landfill’s eastern stormwater sedimentation basin (called the East Basin), an area that is not a permitted hazardous waste storage unit and not authorized to store or hold leachate. Increased rainfall in December 2025 resulted in an overtopping of the weir (a small dam) in the East Basin. As a result, on December 29 and 30, 2025, stormwater mixed with leachate was released to Castaic Creek, which flows into the Santa Clara River.

What’s at Stake?

Several residential communities are near the landfill, including the Val Verde, Halsey Canyon, Halsey Hills, North Bluffs, Live Oak, and Williams Ranch communities. The nearest, the Val Verde community, is located approximately 1,000 feet northwest of the developed area of the landfill. Thousands of residents reside in these communities, and several schools are near the landfill, including two preschools, four elementary schools, two middle schools, and two high schools. In November 2023, local, state, and federal agencies formed a Multi-Agency Critical Action Team, comprised of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the California Environmental Protection Agency (CalEPA), the Regional Water Board, CalRecycle, DTSC, South Coast Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD), and various departments within the County of Los Angeles, among others. To date, there are several ongoing administrative and court enforcement actions stemming from the Multi-Agency Team’s efforts to address the ever-increasing impacts of the subsurface elevated temperature event, including lawsuits filed by Los Angeles County and SCAQMD. Residents have filed several individual and class-action lawsuits alongside efforts from local leaders to demand greater accountability and relief.

What’s Next?

Today’s lawsuit adds to these existing actions by bringing new claims against the landfill and generating additional momentum towards relief for the environmental and public health harm. In the lawsuit, DTSC bring claims against the landfill for violating multiple sections of the state Hazardous Waste Control Law relating to the management of hazardous waste, and the Attorney General alleges a claim for equitable relief under Government Code section 12607 to protect the natural resources of the state (including its air, water, and soil) from pollution, impairment, or destruction and a claim under Business and Professions Code section 17200, which prohibits businesses from profiting from various activities that constitute “unfair competition” under that law. The lawsuit seeks civil penalties, disgorgement, and injunctive and other equitable relief for these claims and violations, including an abatement fund to help address environmental pollution and ensure protection of the state’s natural resources, which has and will continue to affect the nearby communities.

item.title: Attorney General Bonta Secures Complete Victory in PlayPower/Burke Case, Parties Abandon Merger
item.description:
October 27, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

Merger was expected to lead to higher prices, lower quality in the commercial outdoor playground equipment market

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today issued a statement after PlayPower, Inc. (PlayPower) and BCI Burke Company, LLC (Burke), two of the top five largest national suppliers of commercial outdoor playground equipment, abandoned their proposed merger. A week ago, Attorney General Bonta, as part of a bipartisan coalition of 12 states and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), filed a lawsuit alleging the proposed merger of PlayPower and Burke was illegal, would result in less competition in the market for commercial outdoor playground equipment both nationwide and in California, and could lead to higher prices and lower quality.

“As the fourth largest economy in the world, California has an outsized responsibility in ensuring business practices are fair and competitive — and today, we’ve delivered. Corporate consolidation means big profits for corporations taken out of the pockets of Californians. The end of the proposed PlayPower/Burke merger is a remarkable victory for taxpayers, our schools, local parks and recreation departments, and our kids,” said Attorney General Bonta. “I am proud of the work my office has done in collaboration with the Federal Trade Commission, and I remain steadfast in my commitment to economic justice and protecting an economy where both businesses and families can thrive.”

BACKGROUND

The market for commercial outdoor playground equipment is already highly concentrated, with five main competitors accounting for approximately 85% to 90% of the sales in the U.S. This proposed merger of PlayPower and Burke would have combined two of the top five largest suppliers. With less competition, businesses face less pressure to keep prices competitive and can charge higher prices without improving the quality of goods and without the risk of losing customers to competitors. Purchases of commercial outdoor playground equipment are mostly funded through government and taxpayer dollars, largely by schools and parks and recreation departments, meaning most of the cost of price increases, including those due to reduced competition, would have fallen squarely on the public. In the lawsuit filed last week, the coalition argued that the merger would have substantially lessened competition in market for commercial outdoor playground equipment, in violation of Section 7 of the federal Clayton Act. 

ANTITRUST ENFORCEMENT AND AFFORDABILITY

As many California families are experiencing the burden of the affordability crisis, Attorney General Bonta remains committed to going after anticompetitive behavior driving up costs. In the entertainment and media industries, Attorney General Bonta recently announced a settlement with Paramount in the Warner Bros./Paramount litigation that protects the livelihoods of Hollywood workers and guarantees massive investments in domestic film production and secured a victory in the ongoing Nexstar/Tegna litigation. This past year, he also tackled other anticompetitive conduct by securing an end to Agri Stats’ price coordination scheme that drove meat prices up for consumers, exposed Amazon’s illegal price fixing scheme, and secured a settlement that delivered 8.9 million eggs to California food banks.

Visit our website to take a look at the full scope of our antitrust program.

item.title: All Bets Are Off: Attorney General Bonta Shuts Down Illegal Gambling Ring in Solano County
item.description:
October 26, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.gov

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today announced the results of an illegal gambling bust at a Solano County business. On October 21, 2026, the California Department of Justice (DOJ) seized three illegal multi-player gambling machines in addition to arresting three individuals present at the illegal gambling location.

“Thanks to the hard work and vigilance of our local law enforcement partners and DOJ special agents, we have proven that illegal gambling and criminal activity of any sort will not be tolerated in California. All gaming must be conducted legally and transparently, with no exceptions,” said Attorney General Bonta. “Let this operation serve as a lesson to not bet against the California Department of Justice. If you do, your luck will run out, and when it does, we will not hesitate to prosecute you to the full extent of the law.”

In July 2026, DOJ received a credible tip from the Vallejo Police Department (VPD) that there were illegal gambling establishments operating in the City of Vallejo. Investigators from DOJ’s Bureau of Gambling Control (BGC) reviewed the information and decided to take the lead on the investigation. In a joint effort, DOJ directed the operation and prepared the search warrant, while VPD's SWAT team executed the service of the search warrant. All charges will be filed with the Solano County District Attorney's Office.

BGC’s responsibility is to ensure that gambling in California is conducted honestly, competitively, and free from criminal and corruptive elements. When those requirements are not being met by businesses and/or individuals, it is BGC’s job to step in and uphold the law. 

It is important to note that a criminal indictment contains charges that are only allegations against a person. Every defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty.
